dedupe_keys.name: remote sensing estimates of health facility damage after the february 2023 earthquake in turkey

description: This case tests whether building damage estimates from satellite imagery can tell responders quickly which health facilities were damaged after the February 2023 earthquake in Turkey. The authors overlaid building-level damage outputs from two machine learning models, one from Microsoft and one from Google, with health facility locations, compared the models with each other and with reported damage, and reviewed common errors on selected imagery. The producers are Ramachandran, Yadav and Schroeder, publishing in PLOS Digital Health (2025). Coverage is 25 hospitals, 13 dialysis facilities and 454 pharmacies in three cities of the affected region. Model A flagged 10.4 percent and model B 4.3 percent of facilities as significantly damaged; agreement between them was fair, sensitivity was only 42.9 percent for both while specificity exceeded 93 percent, and results were best for hospitals. Aggregating damage over small areas raised sensitivity to 71.4 and 57.1 percent. Errors came mainly from misidentified buildings and underestimated damage to destroyed buildings. The article is open access and free to read. Caveats: facility locations and ground truth are not released with the paper, and results apply to one event and two model versions. Simulation uses: estimating uncertainty in rapid damage inputs to health system response models, and planning ground surveys where models are least reliable. Related records: SKAI (model-skai) is Google Research's open damage assessment code, and xBD (data-xbd-building-damage) is a labelled damage benchmark.

name: Remote-sensing estimates of health facility damage after the February 2023 earthquake in Turkey
outcomes: For 25 hospitals, 13 dialysis facilities and 454 pharmacies in three cities, model A flagged 10.4 percent and model B 4.3 percent as damaged; agreement was fair (kappa 0.32), sensitivity was 42.9 percent for both and specificity 93.6 and 96.8 percent; aggregating damage over 0.125 square kilometre areas raised sensitivity to 71.4 and 57.1 percent, so the models cannot yet replace ground surveys.
